We are very excited to announce [Wren.jl](https://juliabayes.org/Wren.jl), a new library for probabilistic programming in Julia.

If you're not familiar with probabilistic programming in general, the Wren docs contain [a thorough introduction to the underlying concepts](https://juliabayes.org/Wren.jl/dev/tutorials/beginner/), which you can read before coming back to this!

On the surface, Wren's syntax looks and feels similar to typical PPLs.
Many of the underlying machinery has come directly from ideas which my colleagues and I wrote for the [Turing.jl ecosystem](https://turinglang.org).
However, many of its components have been (re)built with the aim of improving performance, including AD via [Enzyme.jl](https://github.com/EnzymeAD/Enzyme.jl), and potential acceleration on GPUs via [Reactant.jl](https://github.com/EnzymeAD/Reactant.jl).
Wren also utilises a two-stage compilation process, heavily inspired by [Tilde.jl](https://github.com/cscherrer/Tilde.jl), that enables some level of introspection and static analysis of models.

Some of this might understandably feel a little opaque.
So, let's walk through a fairly simple model, expanding on it as we go along in order to introduce some of the new functionality that Wren provides.

## Setup

We're going to write a Bayesian multinomial regression model for classifying the MNIST digits dataset.

Let's set up our data first:

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## A note about the MLDatasets version

As of the time of writing of this post, due to [various compatibility conflicts involving JSON3.jl](https://github.com/quinnj/JSON3.jl/issues/330), the newest versions of MLDatasets and Reactant cannot be loaded together.
This should hopefully be fixed soon, and we will update the blog post when this happens.
However, in the meantime, this post uses [a temporary fork of MLDatasets](https://github.com/penelopeysm/MLDatasets.jl) to circumvent this.
If you are trying to run this code you should also use this fork.

:::

```{julia}
using MLDatasets: MNIST

data = MNIST(split=:train)

# N x 784 matrix of pixel values in [0, 1], one row per image
X = Matrix(Float64.(reshape(data.features, 28 * 28, :))')

# Convert labels from 0-9 to 1-10 for 1-based indexing in Julia
y = data.targets .+ 1

size(X), size(y)
```

We can define our model in Wren with a function wrapped in the `@wren` macro.
Random variables are written with `~`, like most other PPLs.
In multinomial regression, we need to have a 'reference' category against which the other categories are compared, whose logits (i.e. unnormalised 'probabilities') are set to zero.
For this example, we use the the digit '0' as the reference category.

```{julia}
using Wren, Wren.Dists
using LogExpFunctions: softmax

@wren function mnist1(X, y, C)
    N, D = size(X)
    @iid W ~ Normal() size=(C-1, D)  # Weights
    @iid b ~ Normal() size=(C-1)     # Biases
    ref_logits = zeros(1, N)                  #     1 x N
    nonref_logits = W * X' .+ b               # (C-1) x N
    logits = vcat(ref_logits, nonref_logits)  #     C x N
    probabilities = softmax(logits; dims=1)
    for i in 1:N
        y[i] ~ Categorical(probabilities[:, i])
    end
end
```

We can now instantiate the model with our data.
Note that (unlike in Turing.jl) passing `y` as an argument to `mnist1` alone does not make it an observation; it merely makes the values available to the model.
So, we need to additionally condition the model on `y` using the `|` operator.
Conditioning means that any `y... ~ dist` is treated as an observation in the model.

```{julia}
model = mnist1(X, y, 10) | (; y = y)
```

We can draw from the prior of the model using `simulate`:

```{julia}
simulate(model)
```

This returns a set of the parameters `W` and `b`, together with their associated log-probabilities; precisely the information we need to start performing inference.
For example, we can feed this model to NUTS, using Enzyme.jl to calculate the necessary gradients of the log-density with respect to the parameters:

```julia
import Enzyme

nuts(model, 1000, 4)
```

(Wren's default AD backend is reverse-mode Enzyme, but you can also specify any AD backend you like via the `adtype` keyword as Wren uses [DifferentiationInterface.jl](https://juliadiff.org/DifferentiationInterface.jl/DifferentiationInterface/stable/) under the hood.)

Wren returns [a `FlexiChain`](https://juliabayes.org/FlexiChains.jl) from its sampling routines, which has many useful tools for analysis and visualisation of the resulting data.
Unfortunately, running this will almost certainly take a long time, if only because the model is very large!
(We've omitted this output from the post because of this.)
Of course, the question is then how can we make this faster!

To illustrate the changes in performance, we'll use Wren's benchmarking tools to help us measure the performance of our model.

```{julia}
import Enzyme

@bmodel model DEFAULT_AD
```

There are several fields here, but for NUTS we are most interested in the `lp_and_grad` field, which tells us the median time taken to evaluate the log-density and its gradient.
One can profile this further, but it shouldn't be a huge spoiler if I tell you that the bulk of the time is spent on the likelihood evaluation, because of the large dataset.

## Optimisation, part 1: handwritten likelihood

Traditionally, when faced with performance issues, one of the biggest tools that people reach for is to directly write out a mathematical expression for the likelihood, in the hope of stripping away the overhead of the PPL machinery.
We can do that with the `@addloglikelihood` macro:

```{julia}
using LogExpFunctions: logsumexp

@wren function mnist_manual(X, y, C)
    N, D = size(X)
    @iid W ~ Normal() size=(C-1, D)
    @iid b ~ Normal() size=(C-1)
    ref_logits = zeros(1, N)                  #     1 x N
    nonref_logits = W * X' .+ b               # (C-1) x N
    logits = vcat(ref_logits, nonref_logits)  #     C x N
    @addloglikelihood sum(logits[y .+ C .* (0:(N-1))]) - sum(logsumexp(logits; dims=1))
end

model_manual = mnist_manual(X, y, 10) | (; y = y)
@bmodel model_manual DEFAULT_AD
```

We can see here that the median time has decreased by a small percentage, which is a good start.
More subtly, the number of allocations has also decreased substantially.
This in turn means that the garbage collector has less work to do, and reduces the spikiness in the time taken to evaluate the log-density and its gradient.
While this is not obvious from the summarised benchmark that `@bmodel` gives us, you can see this if you were to directly profile the `WrenCore.lp_and_grad` function.

This is all very good.
*However*, in the process of doing this optimisation, we have also made the model much less readable.
It's hard to see at a glance that this is indeed a multinomial regression model.
This rather defeats the purpose of using a PPL in the first place: if you wanted to just write a bare mathematical expression, you could have done that in a single function without needing the abstraction of a PPL!

## Optimisation, part 2: using `@batch`

This is where one of Wren's features comes in: the `@batch` macro.
We can simply annotate our original `for` loop with the macro, and Wren will attempt to vectorise the likelihood evaluation:

```{julia}
@wren function mnist_batch(X, y, C)
    N, D = size(X)
    @iid W ~ Normal() size=(C-1, D)  # Weights
    @iid b ~ Normal() size=(C-1)     # Biases
    ref_logits = zeros(1, N)                  #     1 x N
    nonref_logits = W * X' .+ b               # (C-1) x N
    logits = vcat(ref_logits, nonref_logits)  #     C x N
    probabilities = softmax(logits; dims=1)
    @batch for i in 1:N
        y[i] ~ Categorical(probabilities[:, i])
    end
end
model_batch = mnist_batch(X, y, 10) | (; y = y)
@bmodel model_batch DEFAULT_AD
```

The only difference between this model and the original `mnist1` model is the addition of the `@batch` macro.
We see that this allows us to gain the same performance benefits as when we handwrote our likelihood, with no loss in readability!

Hand-written likelihoods, like the one we wrote above, can have a significant impact if it allows us to reduce the number of redundant computations.
For example, if we have `y[i] ~ Normal(mu[i], sigma)` for a large dataset `y`, the `log(sigma)` term does not need to be computed `N` times, and can be factored out of the likelihood.
Just like in our present example, `@batch` _also_ does such optimisations automatically for you, without you having to write out the likelihood by hand!
